757.title: Uppalavanna
757.hook: foremost in psychic power among the nuns, and a survivor of terrible harm, told with care
757.howItsDone: In the Theravada tradition, Khema and Uppalavanna are remembered together as the Buddha's chief women disciples, and the story of Uppalavanna's forest hut is told as the reason nuns were given a dwelling in town.

segments.voice: Yesterday: abyakata, the questions left undeclared. Khema answered King Pasenadi, and later the Buddha gave him the same answer. Your line: the same answer. Today, the other nun named beside her.

Two names. In a short passage of the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha names two nuns as the measure for his nuns: a nun of faith may hope to become like Khema and like Uppalavanna. Khema came yesterday. Today is the other. Her name, tradition says, comes from the blue lotus, the color of her skin. The texts remember her for power. The commentaries also remember a harm done to her that no one should ever suffer. Today touches it once, gently, and spends longer on who she was before it and after it. Her life is not the harm.
screen: `TWO NUNS AS THE MEASURE.` → `NAMED FOR THE BLUE LOTUS.` → `HER LIFE IS NOT THE HARM.`

segments.voice: First, who she is. In the list of foremost disciples, Uppalavanna is named first among the nuns for psychic power, what the texts call iddhi. That title comes from the Buddha. Second, the harm, told the way the Dhammapada commentary tells it, and no further. She was living alone in a forest hut. A man who had long wanted her hid there and forced himself on her. She was already awakened, the story says. The deed was his, and the story treats it as his alone. Tradition says the earth opened and took him. Third, what came after. Some monks wondered aloud whether an awakened person might still take pleasure in such things. The Buddha answered that the awakened cling to sense pleasures no more than water clings to a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed to the point of a needle. She was not stained. And something practical changed: tradition says the Buddha asked that nuns no longer live alone in the forest, and King Pasenadi had a dwelling built for them inside the town. Fourth, her own voice. In the Connected Discourses, Mara, the tempter, finds her standing alone under a sal tree in full flower, and asks if she isn't afraid of rogues. She is not, she answers. She has mastered her mind, and he can't frighten her. That's the Uppalavanna the texts keep: not only what was done to her, but who she was, before and after. She survived.
screen: `FOREMOST IN POWER.` · `A HARM, AND IT WAS HIS.` · `WATER ON A LOTUS LEAF.` · `MARA FINDS HER UNAFRAID.` · then, large: `SHE SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind someone who came through something hard that was not their fault; you don't need the details, those are theirs. Picture the whole person, their laugh, their skill, the way they are now, and if wishing them well comes easily, let it come. If this brushes against something of your own, it's enough to keep breathing, slowly and steadily.
Uppalavanna. The nun named foremost in psychic power, who survived harm that was never hers, and met Mara unafraid. Today's word.
Your line: she survived. A life is always more than its wound. See you tomorrow.

758.title: Patacara the teacher
758.hook: the woman who lost everything becomes a teacher of other grieving women
758.howItsDone: Patacara's verses and the verses of the women she taught are read in the Therigatha, and in Theravada communities her story is told as a teaching on grief and on how short and uncertain life is.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uppalavanna, foremost in psychic power, who met Mara unafraid. Your line: she survived. Today, a survivor who turned around and taught.

An arrow, lodged where nobody can see it. That's how grieving mothers, in the verses of the elder nuns, speak of their sorrow for their children. And they name the woman who drew it out: Patacara. Tradition tells her losses first: a husband, children, parents, all gone, it says, in a stretch of days so terrible that she wandered out of her mind with grief, until she reached the Buddha. That's usually where the telling stops. Today it keeps going. The woman who lost everything becomes the one other grieving women come looking for.
screen: `AN ARROW NO ONE CAN SEE.` → `SHE DREW IT OUT.` → `THE GRIEVING COME TO HER.`

segments.voice: First, her own waking. In her verses in the Therigatha, Patacara tells how she washed her feet, watched the water run down the slope, and steadied her mind on it. The commentary adds what she saw: some water went a little way, some further, some further still, the way lives run short and long. That evening she took a lamp into her cell, sat on her bed, and drew down the wick with a needle. As the flame went out, her mind was freed. Second, what she says to the grieving. In another poem, mothers remember her words. You don't know the way he came, or the way he went. He came from somewhere unseen and went on somewhere unseen. So why weep, crying, my son? It sounds hard on paper. In the poem it lands as the voice of someone who stood in the same place. Third, what the women say back. She drew the arrow from their hearts, they say, the grief for their children, and they went forth as nuns. Other nuns' verses name her too: they did as Patacara taught, washed their feet, went to their cells, and woke. Fourth, the title. In the list of foremost disciples, Patacara is named first among the nuns who know the discipline, the community's rules. The woman who once wandered wild with grief became the keeper of order. Grief didn't vanish. It became a way to recognize someone else's. From grief to teacher.

segments.voice: Think of someone who is grieving now, a loss this year or an old one that still sits close. Patacara didn't lead with answers; she sat with people first, so just keep this person company in your mind, with nothing to fix. Then let them rest there, and come back to your breath.
Salla, a dart or arrow. What grieving women say Patacara drew out of their hearts, the grief for their children. Today's word.
Your line: from grief to teacher. The one who lost everything became the one people came looking for. Until tomorrow.

759.title: Dhammadinna
759.hook: foremost among nuns in teaching; the Buddha says he would have answered as she did (MN 44)
759.howItsDone: The Culavedalla Sutta, Dhammadinna's dialogue with Visakha, is studied in Theravada monasteries and Buddhist study groups as a short, careful teaching on identity, the path and feeling.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salla, the arrow of grief Patacara drew out of other mothers' hearts. Your line: from grief to teacher. Today, a nun whose answers the Buddha stood behind.

A man goes to see a nun, and he brings questions. He's Visakha, a lay follower, and he isn't a stranger to her: the commentaries say she had been his wife before she went forth. Her name is Dhammadinna. He sits to one side and starts asking. What is identity? Where does it come from? What path ends it? She answers each one, cleanly. And he keeps going, question after question, until he goes one question too far. This Visakha, by the way, is a man. The laywoman Visakha comes in a few days.
screen: `A MAN WITH QUESTIONS.` → `HIS FORMER WIFE, NOW A NUN.` → `ONE QUESTION TOO FAR.`

segments.voice: First, the questions, in the forty-fourth discourse of the Middle Length collection. They aren't easy. Visakha asks what identity is, and she answers that the teaching calls it the five aggregates people cling to: body, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. He asks about the noble eightfold path, about meditation, about pleasant and painful feeling and what tendency lies under each one. Her answers are short and exact. Second, the edge. At last he asks: what is the counterpart of nibbana? She stops him. Friend Visakha, you've gone too far; you couldn't find the limit of your questions. The holy life is grounded in nibbana and ends in nibbana. If you wish, go and ask the Buddha, and remember what he tells you. Third, the endorsement. Visakha goes and tells the Buddha the whole conversation. The Buddha says: Dhammadinna is wise, of great wisdom. If you had asked me, I would have answered exactly as she did. That is the meaning; remember it so. Fourth, her title. In the list of foremost disciples, Dhammadinna is named first among the nuns who teach the Dhamma. And notice the echo. Three days ago, Khema answered a king, and the Buddha's answer matched hers. Today the Buddha says it again: the same. The texts make the point twice, on purpose or not: a woman taught, and the teaching stood. She taught him.

Dhammadinna. The nun named foremost in teaching, whose answers the Buddha said he would have given himself. Today's word.

760.title: The mustard seed, after
760.hook: Kisa Gotami becomes a nun known for rough robes and a clear mind
760.howItsDone: Kisa Gotami's mustard seed story is told by Buddhist teachers as a teaching on death and grief, and her verses and her answer to Mara are read in the Therigatha and the Connected Discourses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dhammadinna, whose answers the Buddha said he would have given himself. Your line: she taught him. Today, a story many know, and what came after it.

A young mother carries her dead child from door to door, asking for medicine. The Buddha tells her he can help, if she brings him a mustard seed from a house where no one has ever died. She knocks, and knocks. Every house has its dead. Somewhere along that street she understands, and she lays her son down. That's the mustard seed, as the commentaries tell it. But Kisa Gotami's story doesn't end on that street. She goes forth as a nun, and the texts remember her for two things that sound small: rough robes, and a mind that couldn't be shaken.
screen: `A SEED FROM A HOUSE WITHOUT DEATH.` → `EVERY HOUSE HAS ITS DEAD.` → `THE STORY KEEPS GOING.`

segments.voice: First, where the story left her. In the commentary's telling, she lays her child down in the charnel ground and goes back to the Buddha. Did you get the mustard seed? She's done with the seed, she says; she has seen that death touches every house. And she asks to go forth. Second, the robes. In the list of foremost disciples, Kisa Gotami is named first among the nuns who wear rough robes. Tradition says that means coarse cloth, cast-off pieces gathered from rubbish heaps and charnel grounds, washed, dyed and stitched. Not poverty for show. A life with less to guard. Third, the clear mind. In the Connected Discourses, Mara, the tempter, finds her sitting alone and needles her. Why sit by yourself with a tearful face, like a woman who has lost her son? Are you out here looking for a man? It's a cruel line, aimed straight at the old wound. Her answer is calm. She has gone past the death of sons, she says, and with that, the search for men has ended too. She doesn't sorrow or weep, and she isn't afraid of him. Mara, seeing she knows him, vanishes. Fourth, the thread. The mother who once couldn't put her child down learned to hold everything more lightly: cloth, comfort, even sorrow. Her verses in the Therigatha tell of the deathless path she found. After the seed came a long, plain life, and a mind the tempter couldn't move.

segments.voice: Rest your eyes, or a hand, on one plain thing you use every day: a mug, a coat, a chair, something nobody would ever notice. Kisa Gotami's robe was rag cloth, and she wore it with care. Let this plain thing be enough for a minute, and breathe.
Kisa Gotami. The mother who searched for a mustard seed from a house where no one had died, and instead found the plain truth of loss. Today's word.
Your line: after the seed. Her story didn't stop at the grieving; it went on. That's day seven hundred sixty.

761.title: Sona's ten children
761.hook: a mother of ten, left alone in old age, goes forth and awakens
761.howItsDone: Sona's verses are read in the Therigatha, and in the Theravada tradition she is remembered by her title, foremost among nuns in energy, together with the story of her late start.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kisa Gotami after the mustard seed, in rough robes, with a mind Mara couldn't shake. Your line: after the seed. Today, a mother who began late.

Her poem opens with a number. Ten children, she says, I bore from this body. Her name is Sona. The commentary fills in the rest. Her husband leaves home for the homeless life, and she divides the family wealth among her children, keeping nothing back. Once there's nothing more to hand out, the children stop caring for her. She is old now, weak, and alone in the house she filled. So, with nothing left to give away, she goes to the nuns and asks to begin.
screen: `TEN CHILDREN, ONE BODY.` → `SHE GIVES IT ALL AWAY.` → `OLD, ALONE, AND SHE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: First, her own verses, in the Therigatha. After bearing her children, Sona says, weak and grown old, she went to a nun. The nun taught her the aggregates, the sense bases and the elements, and she went forth. Second, the work. The commentary says she knew she had started late, so she resolved to practice through the day and through the night, as though there were no time to spare. One day the other nuns went out and left her behind to heat the water for their baths. While the water warmed, she walked up and down in walking meditation, and there, the story says, beside the fire and the pot, she woke. Third, her title. In the list of foremost disciples, Sona is named first among the nuns who put forth energy. The title goes to the old mother who started last and was left to mind the water. Fourth, where her poem ends. She speaks of her mind as freed and her task as done. It isn't really a story about ungrateful children; they barely appear. It's about what she did with what was left: a tired body, a late start, a pot of water to heat. She didn't wait to be young again. She began where she was. Never too late.

762.title: Ambapali's garden
762.hook: the courtesan of Vesali refuses a fortune for the Buddha's meal, gives her mango grove to the order, and later becomes a nun
762.howItsDone: Ambapali's meal and gift of her grove are read in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the account of the Buddha's last journey, and her verses on aging in the Therigatha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: viriya, the energy of Sona, the mother of ten who began late. Your line: never too late. Today, a garden.

Chariots on the road outside Vesali, going fast. In one of them rides Ambapali, the courtesan of Vesali. She has just heard the Buddha is staying in her own mango grove, so she drove out, sat with him, and asked him to eat at her house tomorrow. He accepted, by staying silent. Now, heading home, she meets the chariots of the Licchavi princes, the ruling families of the town, and drives straight at them, axle to axle, wheel to wheel. What's going on, Ambapali? The Buddha is coming to her house tomorrow, she says. And the princes want that meal for themselves.
screen: `CHARIOTS ON THE ROAD.` → `SHE INVITED HIM FIRST.` → `THE PRINCES WANT THE MEAL.`

segments.voice: First, the offer. In the Great Discourse on the Buddha's final journey, the princes ask her to give up the meal, and offer her a great sum of money. She refuses. Even if you gave me Vesali and all its lands, she says, I wouldn't give up this meal. The princes snap their fingers: we've been beaten by the mango woman! Second, the Buddha. The princes ride on to the grove and invite him themselves. He tells them he has already accepted Ambapali's invitation. Hers came first, so it stands, even against the princes'. Third, the gift. The next day she serves the Buddha and the monks with her own hands. When the meal is done, she sits to one side and gives the mango grove to the community of monks, with the Buddha at its head. He accepts it. Fourth, later. Tradition says Ambapali herself went forth as a nun. Her verses in the Therigatha look back at her own beauty, part by part, her hair, her eyes, her voice, her hands, and how age changed each one. Verse after verse ends with the same refrain: the word of the truth-speaker is not otherwise. A woman who gave away a lovely grove later let go of her own loveliness too, and wrote it down plainly. The mango grove.

763.title: Visakha's riddles
763.hook: a later story: Visakha keeps her father's ten puzzling rules, such as "don't carry the inside fire outside"
763.howItsDone: Visakha's story is told in Theravada countries from the Dhammapada commentary, and she is remembered by the name Migaramata, 'Migara's mother', the name her father-in-law gave her.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ambapali, who wouldn't sell the Buddha's meal and gave her grove away. Your line: the mango grove. Today, a father's riddles.

A wedding morning. A young woman named Visakha is leaving her father's house for her husband's family in another town. Her father, Dhananjaya, takes her aside with advice, and it comes as riddles. Don't carry the inside fire outside. Don't bring the outside fire in. Give to those who give. Don't give to those who don't. Give to both. Sit happily, eat happily, sleep happily. Tend the fire. Honor the household gods. Her new father-in-law, Migara, overhears, baffled. No fire outside? What if the neighbors need a light? A later story, from the Dhammapada commentary, and before it's over, Visakha will be on trial.
screen: `A WEDDING MORNING.` → `ADVICE IN RIDDLES.` → `THE FATHER-IN-LAW OVERHEARS.`

segments.voice: First, the trial. Some time later, the story says, Migara turns against his daughter-in-law and wants her sent home. She asks that her case be heard by elders who came with her from her father's town, and Migara brings up the riddles as proof that she's strange. Second, the fire. She explains each one. The inside fire is the household's private troubles: don't carry tales of your in-laws' faults to the neighbors. The outside fire is the neighbors' quarrels and gossip: don't bring them home. Give to those who give: lend to people who return what they borrow; and not to those who don't. Give to both: help poor relatives, repay or not. Sitting, eating and sleeping happily mean honoring the elders of the house, and tending the fire means treating them with care, like a flame. Honoring the household gods means caring for holy people who come to the door. Third, the turn. The elders find her blameless. In the commentary, Migara later comes to the Buddha's teaching through her, and tradition says he honored her by calling her his mother. Fourth, what travels. Some riddles are a young wife's duties of their own time. But the first one travels well. A quarrel at home grows when it's carried out; a quarrel next door grows when it's carried in. Visakha kept her father's riddles until the day she could say what they meant. Don't carry the fire out.
